summary: The oldest thing on this map and by far the widest. A published international standard, fourth edition, whose forty-two clauses already contain most of what newer formats are still drafting: rigid body physics with six joint types, spatialized sound with room acoustics, a human skeleton standard, text with fonts, volume rendering, shader bindings, a geospatial component with real coordinate reference frames, an event model for interactivity, a scripting component, and a networked component that shares entity state over a long-established simulation protocol. It also carries a proper conformance clause, which almost nothing else here does. Levels below say native for anything defined in a clause of this standard, since components are how this standard is built; where support depends on which profile a reader implements, the note says so. Three warnings for a standards audience. Its coverage is wide but its adoption is thin, so a cell being filled here does not mean two shipping products interoperate. Its unit of length can be changed by the file, unlike the common asset format, which fixes metres. And its addressing points at a file, not at a shared place, so two people opening the same address get two private copies.

coverage.note: Half of this is answered, and answered by name. An HAnimSite is a grouping node whose stated second purpose is an attachment point for accessories such as jewelry and clothing; it takes children, so a hat or a strap hangs beneath it, and the humanoid node keeps a list of its sites. The names come from the humanoid animation standard that this clause binds in, so the same point means the same thing in two files from two authors, which is more than the common asset format offers. What is missing is the item. Nothing defines a wearable as a separate thing that can move from one avatar to another, there are no fitting or scaling rules for bodies of different shape, there is no ownership, and there is no way to put something on or take it off. coverage.note: The time half is specified better here than in most of this map. Zero is midnight Greenwich time on 1 January 1970, absolute times are seconds in double precision, a whole clause defines the reader's clock and the nodes that follow it, processing an event at a given time may only produce events at that time or later, and everything in one event cascade carries the same timestamp and is treated as simultaneous. Ordering inside one reader is therefore exact and written down. The shared half is absent. The clock is that reader's own, the one networked clause stamps an arriving message with the moment it reached the local machine, and nothing in the standard agrees a clock between two hosts, estimates the offset between them or orders events across them.
